video_title: Why HubSpot’s Co-Founder Is Betting Against the SaaSpocalypse
gist: HubSpot co-founder/CTO Dharmesh Shah (transcribed 'Dharmmes Sha') argues against the 'SaaS apocalypse': frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) want to sell tokens through resellers like HubSpot, models are trending toward fungible infrastructure, and chat assistants are the new browser rather than value-capturers. He details HubSpot's AI re-architecture (system of record plus a graph-based 'system of context'), eval-driven model routing, and Uspot, a consumption-priced CRM for one-person businesses riding record US business formation.

insights.claim: Dharmesh Shah argues AI expands rather than shrinks the software opportunity: AI is just software, and it makes a whole new class of previously unsolvable problems addressable, so some SaaS companies will die but the aggregate market gets bigger.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Supports being selective rather than blanket-short on application software; look for incumbents that can address newly solvable problems.
insights.quote: in aggregate the opportunity is bigger than we've ever like if you're anywhere near like software have the agency and and are entrepreneurial there's never been a better time to build a software company

insights.claim: Shah frames the current AI shift as analogous to the cloud transition: some software companies will fail to make the jump just as some failed to move to SaaS/cloud, which he calls the normal circle of life rather than sector-wide extinction.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Expect dispersion within SaaS — winners and losers — rather than uniform multiple compression; pick names by AI-transition execution.
insights.quote: some software companies will die no doubt just like some software companies did not make the transition into SAS in cloud-based things

insights.claim: HubSpot's original VC pitch thesis was that every P&L line item had a $100B+ software company except marketing, and the internet would turn marketing into a software-shaped problem; Shah now makes the identical argument that AI turns new problem classes into software problems.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: A reusable lens: find P&L categories that lack a large software vendor today but become software-addressable with AI.
insights.quote: every line item on the on the P&L has a 100 plus billion dollar software company name attached to that line item except for marketing

insights.claim: Shah notes that despite strong underlying results, public-market sentiment toward software companies is a 'fog of war' and he describes running HubSpot through the period as best of times, worst of times, with the team focusing on customers rather than the stock.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Management acknowledges the sentiment-vs-fundamentals gap in SaaS valuations, a potential source of mispricing.

insights.claim: Host Joe Schmidt argues the market underappreciates how much opportunity size has grown for vertical/SMB software, since AI adds many new ways to deliver value beyond the low-ACV-plus-payments model vertical SaaS historically relied on.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt (a16z, host)
insights.so_what: Revisit TAM assumptions for vertical SaaS names; AI monetization could layer on top of payments/interchange revenue.

themes.theme: Staying off the labs' Yellow Brick Road

insights.claim: Shah's 'yet' test: if a startup's pitch is 'ChatGPT can't do this' and appending the word 'yet' still makes the statement true, the idea is in the frontier labs' path and likely to be run over.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Screen AI startups and point-solution SaaS for gap-filling features the labs will close; avoid those exposures.
insights.quote: if you can just append uh the word yet to it uh and it still holds water that's a problem

insights.claim: Shah warns against 'measuring the product versus the company': a gap in ChatGPT the product says little about what OpenAI the company could build with a new product line.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Assess competitive threat at the lab-company level (resources, roadmap breadth), not current product features.
insights.quote: chat GPT can't do that. It's like, okay, but can OpenAI the company do that?

insights.claim: Durable opportunities sit where frontier labs face a structural constraint (e.g., regulatory) or an incentive constraint — things they could do but are very unlikely to prioritize.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Favor businesses protected by regulation or by being too small/niche relative to lab ambitions.

insights.claim: Shah, an OpenAI investor, argues OpenAI or Anthropic could go after HubSpot's 3+ billion dollars of CRM revenue but their very ambition makes it highly unlikely they will dedicate themselves to it.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Bull case for mid-sized vertical/SMB SaaS: too small a prize for labs chasing trillion-dollar outcomes; watch for evidence to the contrary.
insights.quote: Are they smart enough? Yes. Do they have ambition? Yes. But it's that very ambition that makes it highly unlikely

insights.claim: HubSpot generates three-plus billion dollars of revenue, per Shah.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Scale reference for HubSpot (HUBS) as an SMB CRM incumbent.

insights.claim: Shah's three business rules include 'never compete with Sam Altman', and he admits HubSpot has accidentally done so, e.g. with its agent.ai marketplace for AI agents, which was too horizontal.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Horizontal AI products (agent marketplaces) are exposed to lab encroachment; vertical/go-to-market focus is safer.
insights.quote: never own a restaurant. Number two is don't ever be a landlord and charge rent. And number three is never compete with Sam Alman

insights.claim: Shah advises builders not to solve horizontal weaknesses of ChatGPT or Claude Cowork such as memory, which will improve, but to apply primitives like a 'second brain' to a specific customer class's problems.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: AI memory/horizontal-feature startups are at high risk; vertical applications of the same capability are more defensible.

themes.theme: Labs as token sellers, models as infrastructure

insights.claim: Having spent hundreds of billions on pre-training, frontier labs' core business is now monetizing that capex by selling inference/tokens, both directly (consumer, Fortune 500 like JPMorgan) and via SaaS companies acting as resellers of inference.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Labs have incentive to empower SaaS distribution partners rather than displace them, supporting a partner/reseller role for incumbents like HubSpot.
insights.quote: how do we sell Infer how do we sell tokens how do we kind of monetize the thing that we've built?

insights.claim: Shah says it is less scary to build around AI now than in 2023: then OpenAI looked like it had an unassailable 'magic elixir', but models are now trending toward commodity-like infrastructure in both pricing and fungibility.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Model-layer pricing pressure benefits application-layer margins; bearish implication for pure model pricing power.
insights.quote: models I'm not going to say they're a commodity but part of the virtue of them being as common as they are is they are infrastructure

insights.claim: HubSpot and most SaaS companies now do use-case decomposition and model routing (OpenRouter-style swapping), so no single supplier controls a crucial ingredient and app companies are unlikely to be 'margined out'.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Reduced supplier power of model vendors protects SaaS gross margins as AI features scale.
insights.quote: as long as you stay off the yellow brick road, it is completely possible now that you're not going to get margined out

insights.claim: Shah treats AI as infrastructure analogous to AWS/cloud compute 15 years ago, on which many independent software businesses will be built.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Expect an application-layer boom on top of AI infra, as happened on top of AWS.
insights.quote: think of um AI as infrastructure in the same way we thought of AWS and and cloud comput as infrastructure 15 years ago

insights.claim: When new models are released HubSpot runs its battery of evals across them and quantifies trade-offs, e.g. losing about 3% of quality points in exchange for latency or cost gains.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Eval infrastructure lets incumbents arbitrage cheaper models quickly, a cost lever on AI COGS.
insights.quote: we lose about 3% of quality points uh but we gain this much in terms of latency or or economic

themes.theme: Chat assistants as the new browser

insights.claim: Shah argues ChatGPT and Claude Cowork are becoming the new browser/OS through which people consume value, and, as with the web browser, the interface owner will not capture the whole application stack.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Counter to the bear thesis that chat interfaces disintermediate SaaS; B2B apps that plug in may retain value.
insights.quote: But if you just look at the kind of chat GPT and cloud cos >> they are the new browsers like this is the way people are consuming value

insights.claim: Shah's interface-value spectrum: at one end apps like Uber Eats/DoorDash where the app is trivial and value lies in the network and logistics; at the other, products that are only interface. He places most business applications toward the Uber Eats end because the work done is what is valuable.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Score SaaS names by how much value lives in the UI vs underlying work/data; UI-heavy products are most at risk from AI front-ends.
insights.quote: the actual thing that's valuable is the work that's happening. The interface is a means to an end.

insights.claim: HubSpot was the first CRM company to launch a connector to ChatGPT, over a year ago, and has one for Anthropic; Shah rejects the view that this erodes HubSpot's long-term value.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: HubSpot is positioning as a plug-in inside AI assistants; watch usage via these connectors as a KPI.

insights.claim: Shah views OpenAI's Dev Day moves to enrich ChatGPT with a marketplace and plug-in architecture as validating the model where companies like HubSpot plug into the assistant layer.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Lab platform openness is a key variable for SaaS; tightening would be a risk signal.

insights.claim: Shah's rule: anything that can be solved deterministically with a structured query should be, rather than burning inference — e.g. revenue from Ireland should be a database query, not an LLM trawling millions of Slack messages.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Systems of record with structured data retain value and offer a cheaper, lower-latency path than pure-LLM approaches.
insights.quote: anything that can be solved with a structured query deterministically, solve with a structured query deterministically. Don't use inference to solve something that a query can solve.

insights.claim: HubSpot is rebuilding its primitives for AI: keeping a structured system of record for known facts alongside a new 'system of context' of unstructured data, likely stored as a context graph, to drive agents and outcomes.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Shows incumbents defending the system-of-record moat while adding unstructured context; track HubSpot's agent product rollout.
insights.quote: there needs to be some persistent mechanism for storing kind of known facts uh and data some sort of system or record

insights.claim: HubSpot's reusable-primitives architecture compounded: its marketing automation workflow primitive gave its sales automation product more capability on day one than rivals had built over years.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Platform primitives lower the cost of new product launches, supporting multi-product expansion economics.

insights.claim: Agentic coding lets incumbents attempt large refactors previously unthinkable — e.g. spending $200,000 on tokens to re-implement a codebase with different primitives or in Rust — and validate them against existing tests/evals.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Technical debt becomes cheaper to retire; incumbents with large test suites may modernize faster than assumed, and AI coding token demand grows.
insights.quote: what would happen if we said we're going to spend $200,000 on tokens to go just redo that

insights.claim: Shah argues incumbents' disadvantage is organizational baggage, not a missing capability; if shed, they keep the assets of distribution, customer relationships, evals and 20 years of code as training data.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Incumbents with mechanisms to bypass bureaucracy (founder-led, innovation labs) are better positioned in the AI transition.

insights.claim: HubSpot Next is an internal startup-within-a-startup that pursues new categories, markets or technologies free of HubSpot's stack and brand rules; successful pieces are absorbed like an acqui-hire, as happened with agent.ai's agent builder becoming a HubSpot product.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: A repeatable internal-innovation pipeline is a source of new HubSpot products; watch for Uspot learnings migrating into core.

insights.claim: Shah, still an IC with no direct reports, says now is the best time he has had in HubSpot's 20 years, an indicator of continued deep founder involvement in the AI product rebuild.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Founder engagement is a qualitative positive for HubSpot's AI execution.

insights.claim: HubSpot launched Uspot, a CRM for one-person businesses, 30 days before recording, monetized from day one on a consumption-based model, and Shah says willingness to put down a credit card has made it his most successful HubSpot launch in that regard.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Early evidence that SMB/solo users accept usage-based AI pricing, relevant to SaaS seat-to-consumption transitions.
insights.quote: the thing I've been really surprised by is uh willingness of for people to put a credit card down on a consumptionbased model

insights.claim: US new business formation hit a record in 2025 of roughly 5.6 million (close to 6 million), and 2026 already exceeded 4 million by August, on pace for another record.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Growing SMB/solo customer base is a tailwind for SMB software, payments and fintech vendors.
insights.quote: in 2025 we had the most number of new company formation the United States has ever seen I think it was like 5.6 million

insights.claim: Per US Census tracking, over 70% of new business formations are now predicted not to hire an employee within two years — the highest share ever and rising.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: A large, expanding solopreneur segment favors non-seat, consumption-priced software and AI tools over per-seat SaaS.

insights.claim: Shah likens the one-person-company market to SMB when HubSpot started, when VCs said no software company besides Intuit had built a multibillion-dollar SMB business — implying solopreneurs are a large under-served market.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Look for vendors building specifically for one-person businesses as an emerging category.

insights.claim: HubSpot chose SMB because it combines enterprise's ability to charge for solving problems with consumer-like scale that avoids revenue concentration, unlike long-cycle enterprise or bimodal ad-subsidized consumer.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Explains the durability of SMB SaaS revenue bases: diversified, paying customers.

insights.claim: A customer survey years before HubSpot's IPO found 20% used Salesforce.com, 20% another CRM and 60% no CRM, prompting HubSpot to launch a free, simple CRM subsidized by its marketing software.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Greenfield, non-consumption markets can be won with free products cross-subsidized by an existing paid line.
insights.quote: 20% um were using Salesforce.com uh another 20% were using some other CRM other than Salesforce.com. >> Yeah. Uh but 60% were not using a CRM at all.

insights.claim: HubSpot expanded into CRM partly defensively, expecting incumbent CRM vendors would eventually move into marketing, so staying a pure marketing-software company was not viable long term.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Adjacent-category convergence is a recurring SaaS dynamic; single-product vendors face encroachment.

insights.claim: Shah says distribution, not building, is now the hardest part for startups — arguably harder than before — because AI makes software so easy to build that the market is flooded with options.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Incumbents with existing distribution and customer relationships gain relative value as building commoditizes.
insights.quote: The one thing that's still hard and I would argue maybe even harder now than it was is distribution

insights.claim: HubSpot's ecosystem strategy, learning from Twitter closing its API to developers, is to be openly transparent with partners about white space it is unlikely to enter and to minimize developers' 'time to joy'.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Partner-ecosystem trust is a moat for platforms; developer-hostile platform shifts are a risk to monitor.
insights.quote: in the same way we think about time to value for the core customers we have to think about time to joy for a developer

insights.claim: Shah believes the winners are those with the shortest iteration time and cheapest learning, and that AI dramatically compresses the cycle of testing ideas with real users.
insights.speaker: Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot co-founder/CTO)
insights.so_what: Favor organizations structured for rapid experimentation in the AI era.
insights.quote: the people that win are the ones that have the shortest uh iteration time and the cheapest learning time
